title: Stellantis Takes Full Control of Thiruvallur Plant, Targets 160% Output Jump
excerpt: The automaker bought out CK Birla Group's stake in its 2017 joint venture and will more than double the Tamil Nadu plant's workforce as it ramps output toward 50,000 units, with exports taking the lead.
body:
• Stellantis India has acquired the remaining stake held by Hindustan Motor Finance Corporation Ltd., a CK Birla Group firm, in their 2017 joint venture, taking 100% ownership of the Thiruvallur car plant in Tamil Nadu.
  • The company plans to lift annual output by more than 160% — from 16,000 units in 2026 to over 43,000 by 2028, with CEO Shailesh Hazela separately guiding toward 50,000 units by 2027.
  • About 60% of the additional production is earmarked for exports, positioning the plant as a Stellantis export hub for Africa and South and Southeast Asia.
  • The buyout, funded through foreign direct investment, adds to nearly ₹11,000 crore Stellantis has invested in India across manufacturing, engineering and localisation.

Stellantis has taken full control of its car-assembly plant at Thiruvallur in Tamil Nadu, buying out CK Birla Group's stake in the joint venture and setting up a more than 160% jump in annual output as it leans into India as an export base. The move gives the Franco-Italian-American automaker sole ownership of Stellantis Automobiles India Private Limited (SAIPL), the vehicle-assembly company it set up with the CK Birla Group in 2017 to bring the Citroën brand to India.

Stellantis India said it has acquired the remaining equity held by Hindustan Motor Finance Corporation Ltd. (HMFCL), a CK Birla Group company, in SAIPL. The transaction was funded through foreign direct investment. It does not touch Stellantis's other Indian manufacturing partnership — the 50:50 joint venture with Tata Motors at Ranjangaon, which builds Jeep models — that entity remains unchanged.

A joint venture that ran its course

The SAIPL partnership dates to 2017, when Stellantis — then operating as PSA Group before the Fiat Chrysler merger — teamed up with the CK Birla Group to establish vehicle assembly in India. Assembly at Thiruvallur began in 2021, and the plant now builds four Citroën nameplates: the C3 hatchback, the e-C3 electric, the C3 Aircross and the Basalt coupe-SUV. Localisation has crossed 95%, and finished vehicles are already shipped to eight markets across four continents, with Africa and parts of South and Southeast Asia among the destinations.

Citroën's Indian journey has been modest so far. The brand holds roughly 0.3% of India's passenger-vehicle market, selling under 7,000 units in 2025 — though recent months have picked up as the company rolled out its "Citroën 2.0" revamp. The buyout removes a layer of joint-venture governance and gives Stellantis a cleaner structure to push that turnaround.

"India remains a key pillar of Stellantis' growth strategy. Having invested close to INR 11,000 crore in the country to build a strong manufacturing, engineering and export ecosystem, we continue to see significant opportunities ahead."

— Shailesh Hazela, CEO and Managing Director, Stellantis India

The production math

Two sets of capacity figures have emerged, both pointing to the same ambition. In its official statement, Stellantis says annual output will rise from 16,000 units in 2026 to more than 43,000 by 2028 — an increase of over 160%. Hazela separately told journalists that output is about 18,000 annually now and should approach 50,000 by 2027, per AckoDrive and Team-BHP sourcing the Economic Times. The direct shopfloor workforce of 610 employees is expected to more than double, with added indirect jobs across suppliers and logistics in Tamil Nadu.

The export tilt is the striking detail. Per the Times of India, Hazela said roughly 60% of the incremental output will be exported and 40% sold domestically — a ramp-up built on India's cost base, maturing component ecosystem and 95%+ localisation to serve markets where Stellantis lacks local assembly.

"As we look ahead, we are committed to driving growth through new product investments, expanded manufacturing capacity, stronger export competitiveness and deeper localisation."

— Shailesh Hazela, CEO and Managing Director, Stellantis India

Why it matters beyond one plant

The deal fits a broader pattern among global automakers: consolidating manufacturing footholds under full ownership as growth markets mature. For Tamil Nadu — already home to Hyundai, Renault-Nissan and Royal Enfield plants — Stellantis's commitment reinforces its position as India's automotive hub, with workforce growth and supplier spillovers rippling through the regional industrial ecosystem.

For the Indian diaspora, the story lands on two fronts. Thousands of Indian-origin engineers and product specialists work in the global auto industry, and Stellantis's export-led expansion widens the corridor for senior talent movement between its Indian operations and global centres. For diaspora investors, the nearly ₹11,000-crore cumulative investment, the export-hub positioning and the deeper localisation are another data point in the case that global OEMs treat India as a production base, not just a sales market.

What to watch next

The key questions now are product-led. AckoDrive notes Stellantis is preparing to introduce its Leapmotor electric-vehicle brand in India — whether the expanded Thiruvallur capacity eventually hosts that, and how quickly export volumes materialise, will decide whether the 160% target is ambition or execution.
